title: Chapter 225 – A Mile on Foot
html:
[Terrace Six to Terrace Seven – Corin]

Corin has forgotten that feet hurt.

He remembers this on the third step of the Loom's far stair, when the arch of his left foot, which has not carried his weight in three hundred years, folds under him with a sharp bright jolt, and he sits down on the boards so hard that the teeth click in his jaw. The pain is astonishing. It is a bright hot nail driven into the sole of his foot, and it is the first thing he has felt in three centuries that was entirely his own.

"Get up," says a voice, not unkindly.

It belongs to the boy with the shaven head. He is perhaps seventeen, lean and grave, with a water skin on one shoulder and a look in his eyes that Corin recognizes with a small cold shock. It is the look of a person who has been shown his own death and decided to be polite about it. The boy puts out a hand, and Corin takes it, and is hauled to his feet like a sack of grain.

"I am sorry," he says. "I had forgotten that one must put the heel down first."

"It's all right."

"I used to know. I was quite a good walker. I walked from the Hall of Nine to the Door every morning, three miles, in all weathers." He winces. "I think the soles have gone soft."

"They'll toughen."

"Will they?"

"I don't know," says the boy. "But my master says that's what you tell people."

Corin laughs.

It is a startled, cracked, wheezing sound, and it embarrasses him. He has not laughed in so long that he has forgotten how the face does it. But the boy does not look away, and after a moment he finds that he is walking again, one step after another, down the long silver plain, with the boy at his elbow and the soft clatter of the Loom dying behind him.

He does not look back.

---

The plain is a mile wide, and it takes them eleven minutes.

He counts. It is a habit of the Hall, where he was taught to measure everything, and it steadies him. One hundred and twelve paces to the first marker. Two hundred to the second. The looms go by in their ranks, tall and dark and silent, and between them the weavers stand with their hands lifted, frozen in the act of passing a shuttle. He has to walk past them. He had not thought of that. He had thought it would be like leaving a room, and instead it is like leaving a graveyard, where every stone has your own face on it.

He knows some of them.

There is a woman in the third rank whose name was Aldith, who used to hum while she wove. There is an old man in the fifth who lost a hand to the Seam and learned to throw the shuttle with his foot. There is a girl of twelve, in a pale smock, with an empty patient face, who was nine when she arrived. He holds her gaze as he passes. It does not blink.

I will come back for you, he thinks.

It is a lie. He knows it as he thinks it. But it is the kind of lie one tells a sleeping child, and he tells it anyway.

"Keep moving," says the woman with the white streak in her hair.

She is at the head of the line, with her stone hand lifted to shade her eyes. She is tall and thin and hard, with a face like a closed door, and Corin has not decided whether he is afraid of her or in love with her. She has the gift, rare in the old, of making people want to be useful.

"The sound," she says. "Do you hear it?"

He does.

It is behind them: a low sweet tidal murmur, like the singing of a very large and very happy crowd. It has grown since they left the platform. It is no longer a hum but a chorus, a vast slow swell of voices in a single mode, rising and falling with the regular pulse of a walking step. He can hear individual lines, now. A woman's high clear soprano. A man's rough baritone. A child's piping, breathless, off-key.

The Refused, thinks Corin. They are inside the Terrace.

"How far?"

"Half a mile."

"We have ten minutes."

"Less," says the old Keeper, grimly. "They are walking faster than they should."

---

Tamsin leads them.

She goes ahead of the line with her staff ringing on the boards, her white hair streaming behind her, her sewn eyes turned straight forward like a bowsprit. She does not need to see. She has walked this plain for four hundred years, and every plank is a word she knows by heart. She moves at the swift sure pace of a woman half her age, and the others follow in her wake: the hooded lady in the gray cloak, the tall woman with the stone hand, the quiet man with the steady hand, the small bright Warden. Corin brings up the rear with the boy.

He watches her back.

It is a narrow back, bent at the shoulders, in a robe of undyed linen and a sash of a thousand colors. He knew her, in the old days. Not well; she was a Keeper, and he was an apprentice, and the gulf between them was as wide as the sea. But he remembers the first time he saw her, in the doorway of the Hall of Nine, with a basket of thread on her arm and a patient, weary smile. She had been twenty-three years old. She had been the youngest Founder's daughter.

She did not have to stay, he thinks.

She could have gone up with the rest.

He has not asked. He does not know how.

At the three-quarter mile the plain begins to slope. The planks are old, here, gray and cracked and bowed with the weight of centuries, and the looms thin out. Ahead, in the mist, a dark shape rises: a wall, tall and narrow, of black stone. In the center of it there is a door, no wider than a man's shoulders, and above the door a lintel carved with a single word.

SEVEN.

"There," says Tamsin.

She stops.

She turns, with a rustle of linen, and faces the party. Her face is calm. The smile is back, the small patient smile of a woman about to say something unwelcome in a gentle voice.

"This is where I leave you," she says.

---

Nobody speaks.

It is Yue who breaks the silence. She does it as she does everything, directly, without ornament.

"You're staying."

"I am the Keeper of the Loom."

"The Loom is feeding the Door. You said so yourself. The Refused are being woven into it." Her jaw is tight. "If you stay, they'll weave you in."

"Yes."

"Then come."

"I cannot." Tamsin lays her staff against the wall. "Do you know what I am? I am the last of the First Founders' children. I am the youngest of the nine who made this Road. And I am the one who made the Loom." Her smile deepens. "A Loom cannot be abandoned by the one who built it. It would unravel."

"Let it."

"It would take the Door with it."

Yue stops.

"I did not tell you," says Tamsin, softly. "It seemed unkind. But the Loom is not only the cloth that binds the Door. It is the tie. It is the one thread that holds the Door shut from below, against what is on the other side. The Founders built it to be unbreakable. But they built it to be held." She lifts her chin. "A hand must hold it. A living hand. Or it slips."

"And they've woven two million people into it."

"They have woven two million threads. They have not woven a hand." Her face is serene. "I mean to be the hand."

Pebble makes a noise.

"You'll die," he says.

"I have been dying for six hundred years, child. I would like it to be useful."

"It isn't fair—"

"No." The old Keeper turns to him, and there is such tenderness in her ruined face that Corin has to look away. "It is not. I had a thread, once, a long red one, that ended at the Door. I saw it in my youth. I wove it, and I set it aside, and I decided that I would never look at it again." A breath. "I looked at it last night. Do you know what it said?"

"No."

"It said I would be of use." She smiles. "It said that I would stand at the Loom in my last hour with a hundred thousand threads in my hands and hold the Door shut for a day, a week, a month, long enough for someone to climb. It was a very short thread. It was a very good one."

She lays her hand on the boy's cheek.

"I would not trade it," she says, "for all the tea in the Orchard."

---

The farewell is brief.

She does it as she does everything, with a minimum of fuss. She kisses Veyra on both cheeks, a dry formal peck, and says something in her ear that makes the hooded woman go rigid. She shakes Jian's hand, once, firmly, and tells him that he is a very bad liar and that she thinks the better of him for it. She hugs Hua. She tells Yue that the streak suits her. She takes Pebble's face between her hands and says nothing at all.

Then she comes to Corin.

He is standing at the back of the line with his hands clasped, in a smock too thin for the cold, and he has not found a single word. He looks at her. She looks at him with her sewn eyes. He sees, for the first time, that the thread is not white at all but silver, a fine bright wire, and that it has been drawn through the lids with a needle of exquisite precision, by a hand that did not shake.

She did it herself, he thinks.

"I made you promises," says Tamsin.

"You did not."

"I did. Silently." Her voice is very quiet. "I told myself I would wake you when the time came. I told myself that no one should have to weave forever. And then it never seemed to be the time, and the years went by, and I got used to your face." The smile trembles. "I am sorry, Corin. I have kept you far too long."

"You gave me tea."

"It was poor compensation."

"It was the only warm thing in three hundred years."

She makes a sound, half a laugh, half a sob. Then she reaches up, and with a delicate precision, as a woman might remove a splinter, takes hold of the silver thread that closes her left eye, and pulls.

It comes away with a small dry rasp.

The lid lifts.

Beneath it the eye is blue. It is a clear, pale, ordinary blue, the color of a winter morning, and it is entirely blind. It rolls, once, in its socket, and then fixes on Corin's face with a vague hungry tenderness. He realizes, with a cold shock, that she is seeing him. Not with the eye. With the thing behind it.

"There you are," she says.

He cannot speak.

"Walk well," says Tamsin. "Eat when you can. Keep your feet dry." She lets the thread fall. "And Corin. Tell Orrin I said he is a fool."

She turns.

She picks up her staff, and walks back down the long gray plain toward the singing, a small bent figure in a robe of undyed linen, with one blue eye open and one silver thread trailing from her fingers. She does not look back. The mist swallows her before she has gone twenty paces.

Nobody moves for a long time.

---

The door to the Seventh Terrace is smaller than it looks.

It is a narrow slot of black stone, hardly wide enough for one, and as Yue puts her stone hand against it it swings inward without a sound, upon darkness. A breath of cold air comes out, scented with ozone and dust. Beyond it there is nothing: a gap, a void, a tunnel of velvet black.

"Fare," says Jian.

He is standing at the lintel, looking at a small iron bowl set into the wall. It holds six grains of salt. They shine like six small stars.

"One year each," he says. "Six grains. There are six of us."

"Five," says Corin.

They look at him.

"I am no passenger," he says. His voice shakes. "I was never counted. I have not been alive for three hundred years. I have no year to give, and the bowl has no grain for me."

"Then you don't pay," says Yue.

"I do not think the door will allow it."

"Then we'll find out."

She reaches for the first grain.

"Wait," says Veyra.

The hooded woman has stepped forward. She puts out her ruined hand and closes it over the bowl, and Corin sees, with a flicker of alarm, that the ring of ember on her palm has begun to glow. It brightens. It flares. She is pressing the burning mark into the iron, and the bowl begins to shiver.

I am the second key, she says. I have not yet used my right.

"What right?"

The right of passage. She closes her eyes. The Founders made the keys to open the Road. A holder of the second key may pass a party of nine without fare. I have not wanted to. It costs me. A breath. But it costs me a day. And I would rather give a day than watch you give seven years.

"Veyra—"

Let me.

The ember flares white.

The grains in the bowl dissolve. One by one, with a faint sweet chime, they sublimate into smoke, and the smoke rises, and coils, and spills out across the threshold in a pale, shimmering veil. It hangs in the arch. It brightens. And through it, slow and cold and clear, a long white corridor opens, lit by a light that has no source.

Go, says Veyra.

Her voice is hoarse. She is swaying. Hua catches her arm and Yue her other, and between them they half carry her through the arch, and the others follow, one by one, into the white.

Corin goes last.

He pauses on the threshold. He is aware, with a vivid dreamlike clarity, of the whole long plain behind him: the looms, the frozen weavers, the silver mist. He is aware of the sound, the vast sweet chorus, now very near. And he is aware, at the edge of hearing, of a single thin clear voice among the thousands. It belongs to a woman, old, stooped, with one blue eye. She is not singing. She is humming, very low, a small cracked, tuneless domestic sound, like a cook over a stove.

He puts his hand against the lintel.

Thank you, he thinks.

Then he steps through, and the door of the Seventh Terrace closes behind him with a sound like the shutting of a book.

---

The white corridor ends in a mirror.

Corin has never seen one so large. It fills the whole end of the passage, from floor to a ceiling lost in dazzle, a single sheet of silver glass without frame or flaw. In it the six of them stand in a ragged line, small and travel-stained, with the hooded woman held up between the Warden and the tall fighter and the boy with the shaven head gripping the water skin like a rope. The corridor behind them goes back and back, receding into whiteness.

"Do not touch it," says Veyra.

She is standing on her own feet again, though barely. Her face is gray and her breathing shallow. The right of passage has cost her more than a day, he thinks. It has cost her something she did not name.

This is the Seventh, she says. The Terrace of Faces. It runs eighty to one. A day here is eleven weeks of the world's. A year is eighty. She draws a breath. Do not look at anything longer than you must. Do not answer anything that speaks to you. And if you see a person you love, remember that they are not here.

"Mirrors," says Yue.

Mirrors, agrees Veyra. Of a kind.

She lifts her ruined hand and lays it against the glass.

The surface ripples. It does not shatter, or crack, or part; it simply goes soft, like a pond into which a stone has been thrown, and the reflections run together, and re-form. And where the corridor had been, there is a hall.

It is vast. It is so vast that Corin's mind slips on it, like a foot on a wet stair. The floor is a plain of black glass, polished to a mirror finish, running to every horizon. The ceiling is a plain of white glass. Between them, in rows, in ranks, in endless regular files, tall standing mirrors rise on slender columns of silver, each one ten feet high, each framed in a different metal. Gold. Copper. Bronze. Iron. Each reflects a different thing.

He sees a garden. He sees a battlefield. He sees a kitchen, warm and bright with lamps, with a table laid for supper. He sees a child's bedroom, a rooftop, a harbor, a ship under sail. He sees a man in a long gray cloak walking away down a road, his shoulders bent, his hand trailing in the dust.

They are not pictures. He knows that, with the same cold certainty that told him Tamsin would stay. They are places. Each mirror is a door, and through each door a person is looking back.

"What do they want?" he says.

To be answered. The cool voice is very low. Each of them is a version of you. A road not taken. A gift refused. They have been waiting a long time for someone to say yes.

Corin looks at the nearest mirror.

It is a plain bronze oval, no bigger than a window. In it there is a young man in a clean tunic, with a brown beard and an easy smile, standing in the doorway of a sunny workshop. A pen is tucked behind his ear. There is ink on his cuff. Behind him on a long bench lie rolls of paper, brushes, a half-drawn map of a coastline Corin has never seen.

The young man looks up. His eyes widen.

Corin, he says.

It is his own voice. It is warm and clear and a little amused. It is the voice of a man who has never been a weaver.

You got out, says the other Corin. I wondered if you would.

You are not real, thinks Corin, very carefully.

Of course I'm not. I'm what you'd have been, if you hadn't stayed. The smile broadens. Orrin offered me a place at the Draughtswoman's side, you know. A real one. To learn the pattern. To draw the Door. And I said no, because I thought he needed his hands. He shrugs. I was wrong. He had plenty of hands. I'd have been very happy.

Don't answer, says Veyra's voice, sharp in his head.

I'm not, thinks Corin.

You are.

He closes his mouth. He had not known it was open.

He turns his back on the mirror, and makes his feet walk, one after the other, away from the sunny workshop and the easy smile. It is the hardest thing he has done since waking. Behind him, in a voice that is hurt and gentle and utterly without reproach, the other Corin calls once more:

I'd have drawn you a better map.

---

They walk for what feels like an hour.

It is difficult to tell. The hall has no sun, no shadow, no change of light. The mirrors go by on either side in their slender columns, and Corin keeps his eyes on Yue's white-streaked head and counts his own steps. Four hundred. Four hundred and one. A woman in a sunlit orchard calls Pebble's name, and the boy flinches but does not turn. A bearded man in a burning tower reaches for Jian, and Jian shuts his eyes. Hua passes a mirror in which a girl of nine sits on the edge of a bed, in a room she does not recognize, and the Warden's face goes white as paper.

Nobody speaks.

At the thousandth step the pattern of the mirrors changes. They are closer together here, and taller, and the frames are older. Dark metal, black with age. And in each one, instead of a garden or a kitchen, there is a person.

They are standing. They are not smiling. They are all wearing the same pale blue robe with cloud embroidery on the cuffs.

"The Sect," says Yue, under her breath.

There are dozens of them. Hundreds. Corin loses count. They stand in their frames with their hands folded, their faces smooth, their eyes closed. He sees an old man with a long white beard. He sees a girl with a scar. He sees a heavy woman with a missing ear. They are all, he understands, pupils of the Azure Cloud Sect. They are all the ones who climbed.

Ye Shuhan's predecessors, says Veyra. Every pupil the Sect has sent in six hundred years. They came this far. They looked in the glass. And they said yes.

"To what?"

To the thing they wanted. Her voice is bleak. A promotion. A cure. A beloved's return. A name. She almost laughs. It was always something small.

"Where are they?"

In the glass. She turns her hooded head. They are not dead. They are not alive either. They are the Seventh Terrace's collection. They stand in their frames, and they are happy, and they are very tired. A pause. They are the cloth that the Loom does not weave.

Corin stares at the faces.

He thinks of the pale blue riders at the gate of the Hall. He thinks of the pupils on the Quay of Bells. He thinks of six hundred years of eager young men and women climbing a stair to heaven, and a long cold hall at the top of it, where someone was waiting to say of course.

"Is this what the Tenth wants?" he asks.

I do not know what the Tenth wants. Her hood does not move. I know only what the Bloom does when it is left alone.

He is about to answer when Hua makes a sound.

It is a small thin gasp, like a cat's. She has stopped dead in the aisle with her mark-hand pressed to her breast, and her face is white, and she is staring at a tall iron-framed mirror on the left. He follows her gaze.

In the mirror, among the rows of the blue-robed, there is a man in a different color.

He is a lean gray man of sixty. He wears a pale blue robe, like the rest, but over it, tied at the throat, a plain brown cloak, thick with the dust of the road. His hair is cropped. His face is lined and tired and kind. He stands at the front of the frame with one hand raised, palm out, in the gesture of a man who has been waiting a long time to be noticed.

And as Corin watches, the lips move. There is no sound. There is no need of one. He reads it as a weaver reads a thread, by feel, in the dark behind the eyes, and he knows that every other mirror in the long blue row has stopped breathing to hear it.

Help me, says Ye Shuhan.
